api/Bicycle.Physics.BicycleSimulator.htm.summary: Class BicycleSimulator Namespace Bicycle.Physics Assembly Bicycle.Physics.dll Integrates the full nonlinear Whipple bicycle equations of motion for a single bike. Allocation-free on the hot path — all intermediate storage is stack-allocated or pre-allocated at construction time. Typical usage: var sim = new BicycleSimulator(BicycleParameters.GameDefault); sim.Step(0.004, new ControlInputs { DriveTorque = -3.0 }); ref readonly var snap = ref sim.CurrentSnapshot(); // snap.RearFrame.Position gives the rear-frame centre-of-mass in world space (Moore frame) public sealed class BicycleSimulator Inheritance object BicycleSimulator Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Constructors BicycleSimulator(in BicycleParameters) public BicycleSimulator(in BicycleParameters parameters) Parameters parameters BicycleParameters Properties Parameters Gets the physics parameters this simulator was constructed with. public ref readonly BicycleParameters Parameters { get; } Property Value BicycleParameters State Gets the current integrator state by reference (no copy). public ref readonly BicycleState State { get; } Property Value BicycleState Methods AddRearWheelSpinDelta(double) One-shot external impulse: add deltaRadPerSec to the rear-wheel spin rate. Used by game-side bump physics to bleed forward speed when the bike brushes an obstacle. NOT used inside the integrator; consumers call this between Step() calls. Convention: RearWheelSpinRate is negative for forward motion, so positive delta = slowdown. public void AddRearWheelSpinDelta(double deltaRadPerSec) Parameters deltaRadPerSec double ClampSteer(double) Clamps Steer to ±maxAbsRadians and zeroes SteerRate only when the wheel is being driven further into the limit. One-sided so the wheel can still swing back toward neutral once it hits the wall. Intended to be called once per step, after Step(), for game-feel steer-stop behavior. Like rolling friction, this is applied OUTSIDE the integrator on purpose. public void ClampSteer(double maxAbsRadians) Parameters maxAbsRadians double CurrentSnapshot() Returns the world-space poses of all four rigid bodies (Moore frame, +Z down) for the current state. The snapshot is cached and recomputed lazily only when the state has changed since the last call. Returns a reference to avoid struct copies on the hot path. public ref readonly BicycleSnapshot CurrentSnapshot() Returns BicycleSnapshot Reset(in BicycleState) Resets the simulator to the given state, clearing the snapshot cache. Call this after constructing UprightAtSpeed(double, in BicycleParameters) to apply the Roll and Pitch perturbations required to avoid the coordinate singularity (gotchas #3 and #8). BikeWorld.AddBike in the Bicycle.World package does this automatically — prefer it over calling Reset directly in game code. public void Reset(in BicycleState initialState) Parameters initialState BicycleState Step(double, in ControlInputs, double) Advances the simulation by dt seconds using a single RK4 step. Hot path — allocation-free. Callers should use dt = 0.004 (250 Hz). rollingFrictionCoefficient applies a post-step linear decay to the rear-wheel spin rate: spinRate *= (1 - k * dt). Defaults to 0 (frictionless) so existing callers see unchanged behavior. Applied outside the integrator to preserve the Meijaard eigenvalue benchmark. public void Step(double dt, in ControlInputs inputs, double rollingFrictionCoefficient = 0) Parameters dt double inputs ControlInputs rollingFrictionCoefficient double

api/Bicycle.World.BikeWorld.html.summary: Class BikeWorld Namespace Bicycle.World Assembly Bicycle.World.dll Orchestrates N independent bike simulations behind a clean event-driven contract. Unity-side code calls Step(double, IReadOnlyDictionary<BikeId, ControlInputs>) once per fixed update, then reacts to OnBikeSnapshot, OnBikeBump, and OnBikeReset events on the main thread. Hard rules (see spec §6.1): Only one MonoBehaviour (BikeWorldRunner) ever holds a BikeWorld reference. No Unity code calls Step(double, in ControlInputs, double) directly. Every method takes a BikeId so N-bike operation is supported from day 1. Event causal ordering (spec §6.1): Snapshot events fire AFTER all simulators have stepped (consistent world-state slice). Bump events fire immediately when injected (per-bike causal ordering). Allocation-free design: OnBikeSnapshot args are cached per-bike and updated in-place. OnBikeBump and OnBikeReset args are always newly allocated (rare events, not on the hot path). articles/architecture.html.summary: Architecture The project is split into three layers: a physics core library, a world orchestrator library, and a Unity presentation layer. Each layer has a strict contract with the layer below it. Layer diagram +----------------------------------------------------------------+ | Bicycle.Physics (pure C#, .NET Standard 2.1) | | +----------------------------------------------------------+ | | | BicycleSimulator (one per bike) | | | | Step(dt, in ControlInputs) | | | | Reset(in BicycleState) | | | | CurrentSnapshot() -> BicycleSnapshot | | | +----------------------------------------------------------+ | +--------------------------------^-------------------------------+ | owns N of +--------------------------------+-------------------------------+ | Bicycle.World (pure C#, .NET Standard 2.1) | | +----------------------------------------------------------+ | | | BikeWorld | | | | AddBike(BikeId, BicycleParameters, FeelPreset) | | | | RemoveBike(BikeId) | | | | Step(dt, IReadOnlyDictionary<BikeId, ControlInputs>) | | | | Reset(BikeId) | | | | event OnBikeSnapshot(BikeId, prev, current) | | | | event OnBikeBump(BikeId, BumpEvent) | | | | event OnBikeReset(BikeId) | | | +----------------------------------------------------------+ | +--------------------------------^-------------------------------+ | ticks at 250 Hz +--------------------------------+-------------------------------+ | unity-v2/Assets/Bicycle/ (Unity 6 LTS + URP) | | +----------------------------------------------------------+ | | | BikeWorldRunner <- ONLY MonoBehaviour touching BikeWorld| | | | FixedUpdate ticks it; pulls inputs from IBikeInputSource;| | | | re-broadcasts events to the Unity event bus. | | | +----------------------------------------------------------+ | | ^ ^ ^ | | | | | | | BikeVisualizer ChaseCamera CourseDirector | | (per BikeId, (follows a (subscribes to | | subscribes for target BikeId) finish/void/bump, | | own snapshots) no singleton) | +----------------------------------------------------------------+ Hard rules These rules are invariants enforced by design. Violating them introduces the singleton / shared-mutable-state patterns that make multiplayer impossible: Only BikeWorldRunner ever holds a BikeWorld reference. Nothing else touches the physics clock. No Unity code calls BicycleSimulator.Step() directly. All simulation goes through BikeWorld. No Unity component is a singleton. Every system takes a BikeId at Awake or subscribes to an event. Singletons break N-bike operation. The pose stream contract is BodyPose. Unity does not bake in flat-ground assumptions. The 3D Vec3D Position + QuatD Orientation contract is valid for future terrain work. Tick model The physics runs at a fixed 250 Hz (4 ms timestep). Unity's variable frame rate is decoupled from the physics step: BikeWorldRunner.FixedUpdate() calls BikeWorld.Step(Time.fixedDeltaTime, inputs) once per physics step. Time.fixedDeltaTime is set to 0.004 in Project Settings. BikeVisualizer.Update() interpolates between the previous and current snapshot for smooth rendering at any frame rate ("Fix Your Timestep!" pattern by Glenn Fiedler). The interpolation parameter alpha = (Time.time - lastFixedTime) / Time.fixedDeltaTime is computed per frame, kept in [0, 1]. Event causal ordering BikeWorld.Step() follows a two-phase event firing strategy (spec §6.1): Phase 1: step all simulators, capture (prev, current) snapshot pairs. Phase 2: fire OnBikeSnapshot for each bike — after ALL bikes have stepped. This ensures observers see a consistent world-state slice. Bump events (OnBikeBump) fire immediately when injected, not deferred, because they represent a causal per-bike occurrence rather than a world-state slice. Allocation-free design The hot path (250 Hz per bike) is allocation-free: BicycleSimulator.Step() uses stackalloc for the LU solve and a cached delegate to avoid per-step GC pressure. BikeSnapshotEventArgs is cached per-bike inside BikeWorld and updated in-place before each event raise. Subscribers must copy data synchronously — storing a reference across event calls will see stale data. The _stepBuffer list backing array is grown once on AddBike and never shrinks. The allocation-free invariant is CI-gated: a test runs 100,000 simulator steps and asserts GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() is unchanged. articles/glossary.html.summary: Glossary Key terms used throughout this project. Code and prose use the descriptive English names (RearFrame, FrontWheel, etc.) — math notation from the literature appears only in derivation comments. Four rigid bodies RearFrame The rear part of the frame plus the rider. The rider's mass is absorbed into RearFrame; there is no separate rider body. Also called "body C" in Moore's notation or "body B/C" in Meijaard's. RearWheel The rear wheel. Axisymmetric, rolls without slipping on flat ground. Two inertia parameters: IAxial (spin axis) and IDiametral (any perpendicular axis). Also called "body D" in Moore's notation or "body R" in Meijaard's. FrontFrame The fork, handlebars, and any front-mounted mass. Connected to RearFrame via a revolute joint about the steer axis. Also called "body E" in Moore's notation or "body H" in Meijaard's. FrontWheel The front wheel. Same inertia structure as RearWheel. Connected to FrontFrame via a revolute joint about the wheel's hub. Also called "body F" in Moore's notation or "body F" in Meijaard's. Coordinate systems Moore frame The coordinate system used by the generated equations of motion and by BodyPose.Position. +X is forward, +Y is right, +Z is down (into the ground). Named after Jason K. Moore, whose PhD thesis our derivation follows. World frame (Unity) Unity's coordinate system: +X is right, +Y is up, +Z is forward (right-hand, Y-up). PhysicsBridge.ToUnity maps Moore (X, Y, Z) to Unity (X, Z, -Y). Steer axis The axis about which the front frame rotates relative to the rear frame. Tilted by the steer-axis tilt angle lambda from the world vertical. For the Meijaard benchmark bicycle, lambda = 18 degrees. Bicycle model Whipple model The canonical mathematical model of a bicycle, consisting of four rigid bodies connected by revolute joints and constrained to roll without slipping on flat ground. Originally formulated by Whipple (1899); the Meijaard 2007 paper provides the linearized benchmark we validate against. Holonomic constraint A constraint on positions (not velocities). The Whipple model has one: the front-wheel contact point lies on the ground plane. After imposing this constraint, the front-frame pitch is determined by the other generalized coordinates. Nonholonomic constraint A constraint on velocities that cannot be integrated to a position constraint. The Whipple model has four: no longitudinal slip per wheel (2) and no lateral slip per wheel (2). These reduce the number of independent generalized speeds from 6 to 3. Generalized coordinates / speeds The Lagrangian description of the system state. 8 generalized coordinates in BicycleState (XGround, YGround, Yaw, Roll, Pitch, RearWheelAngle, Steer, FrontWheelAngle) with Pitch as a dependent coordinate. 3 independent generalized speeds: RollRate, SteerRate, RearWheelSpinRate. Self-stable window The range of forward speeds at which all eigenvalues have negative real part — the bike spontaneously returns to upright after a perturbation without rider input. For the Meijaard benchmark bicycle: approximately 4.3 m/s to 6.05 m/s. Weave mode The unstable oscillatory mode at low speeds. A complex conjugate pair with positive real part below the low end of the self-stable window (~4.3 m/s). Manifests as a growing side-to-side wobble. Capsize mode The mildly unstable real mode at high speeds. A single real eigenvalue with small positive real part above the high end of the self-stable window (~6.05 m/s). Manifests as a slow lean to one side. Caster mode The heavily damped real mode. Large negative real part at all speeds. Associated with the steer angle snapping back to center — the caster effect of the front fork geometry (trail). Kane's method The multibody dynamics formulation used to derive the equations of motion. Chooses generalized speeds, applies virtual velocities, and produces a compact form that is efficient for both symbolic derivation and numerical evaluation. Moore's thesis derives the full nonlinear bicycle EOM via Kane's method using PyDy. SymPy + PyDy The Python libraries used for symbolic derivation. SymPy is the symbolic algebra engine; PyDy (tools/eom-codegen/derive.py) implements Kane's method on top of SymPy's reference-frame mechanics. The output is pickled symbolic expressions passed to emit_csharp.py. Common-subexpression elimination (CSE) sympy.cse() factors out repeated subexpressions in the EOM, reducing the FLOP count by ~10x. The emitted C# declares numbered temporaries x0, x1, ... at the top of each function. API / runtime BicycleSimulator The per-bike simulation object. Owns one BicycleState, one Integrator, and a cached DerivativeProvider delegate. The step cost is ~3 µs on a modern CPU. BicycleParameters Geometry + inertia POD struct. MeijaardBenchmark is the locked benchmark preset. GameDefault is the tuning surface. BicycleState The 11-double integrator state. 8 generalized coordinates + 3 generalized speeds. Bit-blittable — safe to use with MemoryMarshal.AsBytes. ControlInputs The 3-double per-step torque inputs: SteerTorque, DriveTorque, RiderLeanTorque. See Gotchas 4 + 9 for the sign-convention inversions. BicycleSnapshot The per-step output: four BodyPose values (one per rigid body) plus ForwardSpeed and SimulationTime. BodyPose Position + orientation + linear + angular velocity for one rigid body, in the Moore world frame. BikeWorld The N-bike orchestrator in Bicycle.World. One BikeWorld instance per scene; only BikeWorldRunner holds a reference. BikeId A stable per-bike integer identity. Every N-bike-facing API takes a BikeId to ensure multiplayer readiness. FeelPreset Tunable feel parameters including SteerTorqueScale and DriveTorqueScale. FeelPreset.Default matches the empirically tuned Phase 2 values (-1.5 and -3.0 respectively) that compensate for the sign-convention inversions. Testing Eigenvalue benchmark The pass/fail gate comparing numerically linearized eigenvalues of the simulation to Meijaard 2007 Table 2. Tolerance: <1% relative error (actual: ~1e-6). Run by EigenvalueBenchmarkTests. Allocation-free gate AllocationFreeTests runs 100,000 Step() calls and asserts GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() is unchanged. Fails if any new managed heap allocation is introduced on the hot path. Determinism gate DeterminismTests runs two simulators from identical initial states and asserts bit-identical output. Per-machine bit-exact; cross-machine bit-exactness is explicitly out of scope.

articles/gotchas.html.summary: Gotchas This page documents every known pitfall that cost real debugging time. Organized by phase. Closed issues are marked. These gotchas are canonical debugging shortcuts. Future developers (and dispatched agents): read the relevant section before touching the code. Phase 1 Gotchas (Physics derivation) Gotcha 1: Inertia-tensor rotation direction inverted in derive.py Status: Closed (fixed in Phase 1) Moore's RearFrame/FrontFrame inertia is computed from Meijaard's via R_y(lambda) * I * R_y(lambda)^T where the rotation goes C-frame to world, not the other way around. The eigenvalue benchmark caught it (~16% error on a benchmark eigenvalue at v=0). If a large systematic discrepancy appears after a derivation change, suspect this first. Gotcha 2: Pitch convention at upright is Pitch = SteerAxisTilt, NOT Pitch = 0 Status: Closed (fixed in Phase 1) The front-wheel-on-ground holonomic constraint with Roll = Steer = 0 solves to q5 = lambda for the canonical benchmark geometry. BicycleState.UprightStationary correctly sets this. Gotcha 3: Coordinate singularity at exactly Roll = 0 Status: Open (by design — documented workaround) The dependent yaw rate in the nonlinear EOM contains a 1/sin(Roll) factor. Evaluating at exact upright produces NaN. Workarounds applied: LinearizationExtractor perturbs by baseRoll = 1e-3 rad before central differences. All behavioral and determinism tests perturb the initial state by 1e-3 rad in Roll. BikeWorld.AddBike applies Roll = 1e-3 automatically. Gotcha 4: ControlInputs.DriveTorque sign convention is inconsistent Status: Open (documented — scheduled for Phase 3 fix) The docstring says "Negative = brake", but the generated EOM treats positive DriveTorque as decelerating. Phase 1 behavioral test Scenario 5 papered over this by negating the test's input. FeelPreset.Default uses DriveTorqueScale = -3.0 to compensate. Any new input source must apply the same compensation until the EOM mapping is fixed in Phase 3. Gotcha 5: KanesMethod returns a 6×6 augmented mass matrix Status: Closed (by design) KanesMethod returns a 6×6 augmented mass matrix when nonholonomic constraints are present, not the 3×3 reduced system the plan originally assumed. The generated code uses an in-place LU solve with stackalloc Span<double> to keep allocations zero. Gotcha 6: Generated C# is huge Status: Closed (by design) WhippleEOM.cs is ~1100 lines of straight-line FLOPs after SymPy CSE. Do not hand-edit; regenerate via tools/eom-codegen/. See Build & Test Reference. Phase 2 Gotchas (Unity integration) Gotcha 7: Moore frame is +Z DOWN, not up Status: Closed for unity-v2 (PhysicsBridge round-trip tests gate this). Open for legacy unity/. The comment on BicycleParameters.ComZ says "paper places +Z up" — true for Meijaard's paper, but the Moore frame used internally by the generated EOM has +Z pointing down into the ground. PhysicsBridge.ToUnity maps physics (X, Y, Z) to Unity (X, Z, -Y). If a body shows up underground in Unity, suspect this first. Gotcha 8: BicycleState.UprightAtSpeed needs Pitch perturbation Status: Open (documented workaround in BikeWorld.AddBike) BehavioralScenarioTests.MakeInitialState sets s.Pitch = p.SteerAxisTilt + 1e-5 to break a 0/0 in the holonomic constraint at exact upright. Without this extra perturbation the simulator NaNs by the second step. BikeWorld.AddBike applies both the Roll and Pitch perturbations automatically. Any new direct consumer of UprightAtSpeed must apply them too. Gotcha 9: SteerTorque sign convention is also inverted Status: Open (documented — scheduled for Phase 3 fix) Same issue as Gotcha 4 but for steer. DebugInputProvider works around it with _steerTorqueScale = -1.5. FeelPreset.Default uses SteerTorqueScale = -1.5. Gotcha 10: Whipple model has no ground-contact constraint for off-nominal states Status: Open (Phase 4 territory) When Roll grows past ~30–40°, the model is outside its valid range. The integrator continues until Roll = 0 is crossed and the 1/sin(Roll) singularity NaNs everything. BikeWorldRunner auto-resets on NaN AND on |Roll| > 1 rad. The bike does not physically rest on the ground after falling — that requires a contact extension (Phase 4). Gotcha 11: MCP for Unity's read_console does not surface Debug.Log entries Status: Closed (workaround documented) Only errors, warnings, and exceptions come through read_console. For runtime print debugging, tail ~/AppData/Local/Unity/Editor/Editor.log directly — it captures everything. Gotcha 12: manage_prefabs create_from_gameobject cannot overwrite an existing prefab path Status: Closed (workaround documented) It silently creates a sibling <name> 1.prefab and leaves the old one in place. Pattern that works: ask the user to delete old, rename new, then mcp__UnityMCP__refresh_unity --mode force. Gotcha 13: Prefab/scene reference IDs reset when GameObjects are deleted and recreated Status: Closed (workaround documented) If you manage_gameobject delete RearFrame and create a new one, every component that referenced the old RearFrame Transform goes null. Re-wire via set_property after rebuilding. Gotcha 14: Unity primitive Cylinder's mesh +Y axis is its height axis Status: Closed (workaround documented) For wheel visualization, treat the wheel GameObject as a parent driven by physics, with a child Cylinder primitive rotated (0, 0, 90) so the cylinder's height aligns with the spin axis. Driving the wheel directly with BodyPose.Orientation (which includes accumulated spin angle) makes the cylinder symmetry axis tumble. Gotcha 15: Yaw sign bug in the kinematics Status: FIXED 2026-05-14 Root cause: SymPy's frame.dcm(N) returns a world→body rotation matrix, but the C# QuatFromMatrix helper expected body→world. The codegen was passing C.dcm(N) directly, producing an inverse rotation. Fixed by a transpose in tools/eom-codegen/emit_csharp.py. Regression test: BehavioralScenarioTests.RearFrameForwardAlignsWithRearWheelVelocity_Under_Sustained_Steer. Phase 2.6 Gotchas (Unity v2 rebuild) Gotcha 16: Do NOT pass -quit to Unity batchmode when using -runTests Status: Closed (documented) Unity Test Framework manages its own exit lifecycle. Passing -quit causes Unity to shut down during initial asset import, before tests execute. Correct for -runTests: Unity.exe -batchmode -nographics -projectPath <path> -runTests -testPlatform EditMode -testResults <xml> -logFile <log> — no -quit. Correct for -executeMethod: include -quit. Gotcha 17: Local Unity 6000.3.15f1 rewrites ProjectVersion.txt on every project open Status: Closed (documented) The pinned version in unity-v2/ProjectSettings/ProjectVersion.txt is 6000.0.40f1 (LTS). Local development on 6000.3.15f1 works but always run git restore unity-v2/ProjectSettings/ProjectVersion.txt before committing. Gotcha 18: Unity Quaternion is single-precision float; orientation round-trip tests need 1e-6 tolerance Status: Closed (documented, tests use separate tolerance constants) Position round-trips can stay at 1e-9 (sign flips + component swaps only). Orientation round-trips need 1e-6 tolerance due to float precision loss in cos(pi/4) / sin(pi/4). Gotcha 19: Unity Editor -executeMethod requires fully qualified namespace Status: Closed (documented) -executeMethod SandboxSceneBuilder.BuildAll fails silently with exit code 1. Correct form: -executeMethod Bicycle.Editor.SandboxSceneBuilder.BuildAll. Gotcha 20: Inspector wiring is not yet automated for Sandbox.unity Status: Open — scheduled for v2.1 polish The scene exists with a BikeWorldRunner GameObject, but the BikeConfig list is empty. Press-Play in Editor will not yet show a moving bike until a BikeConfig is wired via Inspector. The PlayMode test bypasses this via runtime construction. Gotcha 21: KeyboardInputSource.FeelPreset null fallback uses 1.0 scales, NOT the negative defaults Status: Open — scheduled for v2.1 polish When no BikeFeelPresetAsset is assigned, the source defaults to scale = 1.0 — which means W decelerates and steer is inverted (per Gotchas 4 + 9). For correct keyboard mapping, you MUST assign a BikeFeelPresetAsset with explicit SteerTorqueScale = -1.5, DriveTorqueScale = -3.0.

articles/overview.html.title: Overview | Bike — Whipple bicycle simulator + Unity game
articles/overview.html.summary: Overview A multiplayer bicycle game where the physics is honest and the game is hard. Bike is a small multiplayer game in the spirit of Flappy Bird, Getting Over It, and Baby Steps — but on a bike. The bike's balance comes from real bicycle dynamics, not Unity's stock rigidbody simulator. The difficulty comes from the rider's coordination problem: stay upright, pedal in rhythm, don't fall. Why this is interesting A real bicycle isn't balanced by the rider — it's balanced by physics. Hold it at the right speed and the bike will keep itself upright. Go too slow and it falls. Go too fast and you get high-frequency wobble. This genuinely surprising behavior emerges from a 4-body rigid-body system with no-slip rolling constraints, and it's what makes a bike interesting to ride. Capturing it correctly in a game is rarely done — most "bike" games use simplified inverted-pendulum hacks. This project uses the full equations. The system has four rigid bodies connected by two revolute joints and constrained to roll without slipping on flat ground: + steer axis (tilted by λ) / / ┌─────FrontFrame─────┐ │ │ │ RearFrame│ FrontWheel │ │ │ RearWheel● ● ● │ │ │ ════╪════════════╪════ ground (z = 0) │ │ After applying the holonomic ground-contact constraint and the four nonholonomic rolling constraints, the system has three dynamic degrees of freedom: Roll angle of the rear frame (lean) Steer angle (front frame relative to rear) Rear wheel spin angle (forward speed) Everything else — yaw, pitch, position, front wheel spin — is determined by integrating these three plus the constraint equations. Game vision The eventual product is a small multiplayer game where players struggle to keep their bikes upright while pedaling around a shared world. The design pillars: Intentionally hard. Hard does NOT mean unfair — the bike's balance physics is honest; the difficulty comes from the rider's coordination problem. Bike feel is the acceptance gate. Every phase is blocked on "does the bike feel right?" before the next phase starts. Physics does the punishing. No game-logic fall triggers. The bike falls because the physics says it fell — lean past the stability envelope and the equations do the rest. Performance headroom from day one. The physics runs at 250 Hz, allocation-free, at ~3 µs per step. The budget supports 100 bikes on screen simultaneously at 60 fps. Two libraries, one game The project is split into two pure-C# libraries and a Unity presentation layer: Layer Project Purpose Physics core Bicycle.Physics Deterministic, allocation-free Whipple EOM integration World orchestrator Bicycle.World N-bike event-driven contract, no Unity dependency Presentation unity-v2/ MonoBehaviours, rendering, input, scene wiring See Architecture for the full layer diagram and design rationale. Current state (as of 2026-05-20) Milestone Status Phase 1: Physics core Done — 67 tests, eigenvalues match Meijaard 2007 to 6 decimal places Phase 2: Unity MVP Done — Sandbox scene, BicycleController, HUD, ragdoll fall Phase 2.5: DeskCourse MVP Done — first playable level, leaderboard v2.0 Walking Skeleton Done — clean unity-v2 rebuild on Unity 6 LTS + URP v2.1 Mobile / WebGL In progress See Phase History for the full milestone log. References Meijaard, Papadopoulos, Ruina, Schwab. Linearized dynamics equations for the balance and steer of a bicycle: a benchmark and review. Proc. R. Soc. A 463 (2007). Moore, J.K. Human Control of a Bicycle. PhD thesis, UC Davis, 2012. PyDy bicycle validation example: https://github.com/pydy/pydy/tree/master/examples/bicycle_validation Glenn Fiedler, "Fix Your Timestep!" https://gafferongames.com/post/fix_your_timestep/

articles/whipple-model.html.summary: Whipple Bicycle Model The physics core implements the canonical Whipple bicycle model — the same model used in the Meijaard et al. 2007 benchmark paper and Moore's 2012 PhD thesis. Our implementation matches the published eigenvalues to six decimal places. The four rigid bodies The bicycle is modeled as four rigid bodies: + steer axis (tilted by lambda) / / +---------FrontFrame---------+ | | | RearFrame | FrontWheel | | | RearWheel * * * | | | ========+================+==== ground (z = 0) | | RearFrame — the rear part of the frame + rider (rider mass absorbed into RearFrame) RearWheel — axisymmetric wheel, rolls without slipping on flat ground FrontFrame — fork + handlebars + front mass FrontWheel — axisymmetric wheel, rolls without slipping on flat ground The two frames are connected by a revolute joint about the steer axis (tilted by the steer-axis tilt angle lambda from world Z). Each wheel is a revolute joint about its hub. Degrees of freedom After applying: 1 holonomic constraint (front wheel contact point lies on the ground plane) 4 nonholonomic constraints (no longitudinal slip per wheel, no lateral slip per wheel) The system has 3 dynamic degrees of freedom: \(\phi\) — lean (roll) of the rear frame \(\delta\) — steer angle (front frame relative to rear) \(\theta_R\) — rear wheel spin angle (sets forward speed via the rolling constraint) Everything else — yaw, pitch, XY ground position, front wheel spin — is determined by integrating these three plus the constraint equations. Linearized dynamics (Meijaard 2007) Near the upright equilibrium, the lean/steer dynamics reduce to a 2-DOF linear system that depends only on forward speed \(v\) and gravity \(g\): \[ \mathbf{M}\,\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + v\,\mathbf{C}_1\,\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \left(g\,\mathbf{K}_0 + v^2\,\mathbf{K}_2\right)\,\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{f}, \qquad \mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix}\phi\\\delta\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{f} = \begin{bmatrix}T_\phi\\T_\delta\end{bmatrix} \] Where: \(\mathbf{M}\) is the symmetric positive-definite mass matrix \(\mathbf{C}_1\) captures gyroscopic and centrifugal effects (scales linearly with \(v\)) \(\mathbf{K}_0\) is the gravity-driven stiffness/instability matrix \(\mathbf{K}_2\) captures castering forces (scales with \(v^2\)) All four are constant 2×2 matrices computed once from the bike's geometry and inertia parameters. Self-stability: the key result The free-response eigenvalues come from: \[ \det\left(\lambda^2\,\mathbf{M} + \lambda\,v\,\mathbf{C}_1 + g\,\mathbf{K}_0 + v^2\,\mathbf{K}_2\right) = 0 \] Plot the real parts against forward speed \(v\) for the benchmark bicycle: Re(lambda) | 5 | \ <- capsize mode (real) | \\ weave mode (real part of complex pair) 0 |---\----\----------------------------/---- <- stable (Re < 0) | \ \ / -5 | \ \----------------------- | \ caster <- caster mode -10| \___________________ | | | | | | | 0 v_w ~4.3 v_c ~6.05 10 v (m/s) <-- self-stable --> Between approximately \(v_w \approx 4.3\) m/s and \(v_c \approx 6.05\) m/s, every eigenvalue has negative real part — the bike spontaneously returns to upright after a perturbation. This is not a game mechanic; it falls out of the equations. Full nonlinear equations (what we integrate) The linearized form is for analysis. For the game we integrate the full nonlinear equations from Kane's method. After choosing three independent generalized speeds — roll rate, steer rate, rear-wheel spin rate — the dynamics reduce to: \[ \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\,\dot{\mathbf{u}}_{\text{ind}} = \mathbf{f}\left(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{u}_{\text{ind}}, \mathbf{T}\right) \] Where \(\mathbf{M}\) is a configuration-dependent 3×3 mass matrix and \(\mathbf{f}\) packs gravity, gyroscopic, centripetal, and applied-torque terms. The expressions for \(\mathbf{M}\) and \(\mathbf{f}\) are enormous — pages of symbolic algebra — but they're derived once by SymPy + PyDy, simplified with common-subexpression elimination, and emitted as straight-line C# (~3000 FLOPs, zero branches). See Build & Test Reference for the codegen pipeline. Rolling constraints The wheels obey no-slip rolling on the ground: \[ v = -\omega_R\,r_R, \qquad v_F = -\omega_F\,r_F \] The sign is a convention — forward motion produces a "negative" spin rate under our right-hand-rule choice about the wheel's spin axis. This produces the ControlInputs.DriveTorque sign-convention gotcha documented in Gotcha 4. RK4 integration Fixed-timestep classical Runge-Kutta 4th order: \[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{k}_1 &= \mathbf{f}(t_n,\,\mathbf{y}_n) \\ \mathbf{k}_2 &= \mathbf{f}\!\left(t_n + \tfrac{h}{2},\,\mathbf{y}_n + \tfrac{h}{2}\mathbf{k}_1\right) \\ \mathbf{k}_3 &= \mathbf{f}\!\left(t_n + \tfrac{h}{2},\,\mathbf{y}_n + \tfrac{h}{2}\mathbf{k}_2\right) \\ \mathbf{k}_4 &= \mathbf{f}(t_n + h,\,\mathbf{y}_n + h\,\mathbf{k}_3) \\ \mathbf{y}_{n+1} &= \mathbf{y}_n + \tfrac{h}{6}\!\left(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4\right) \end{aligned} \] With \(h = 4\) ms (250 Hz). RK4's truncation error is \(O(h^5)\) per step / \(O(h^4)\) global; for bike dynamics (slowest modes ~1 Hz), this is wildly oversampled. Eigenvalue verification After implementing the full nonlinear dynamics, we numerically linearize via central differences and compute eigenvalues with MathNet's EVD routine. At \(v = 0\): \[ \lambda = \pm 3.131642336,\; \pm 5.530940783 \quad [\text{rad/s}] \] vs. the published Meijaard 2007 values \(\pm 3.131643247906{56},\; \pm 5.530943717653{93}\). Six-decimal agreement. This is the EigenvalueBenchmarkTests gate. Coordinate singularity The nonlinear EOM contains a \(1/\sin(\phi)\) factor in the dependent yaw rate (from the rolling constraint with lateral slip = 0). This diverges at \(\phi = 0\) (exactly upright). Workarounds applied throughout the codebase: BicycleState.UprightStationary sets Roll = 0, but callers must perturb by ~1e-3 rad before simulating. BicycleState.UprightAtSpeed sets RearWheelSpinRate correctly; callers must also set Pitch = SteerAxisTilt + 1e-5 (see Gotcha 8). BikeWorld.AddBike applies both perturbations automatically (Roll = 1e-3, Pitch = SteerAxisTilt + 1e-5). See Gotcha 8. Parameter set The BicycleParameters struct holds the full geometry and inertia set. The static MeijaardBenchmark preset is transcribed verbatim from Meijaard et al. 2007 Table 1 and must not be changed — it is validated by the eigenvalue gate. GameDefault starts equal to MeijaardBenchmark and is the tuning surface for feel iteration. References Meijaard, Papadopoulos, Ruina, Schwab. Linearized dynamics equations for the balance and steer of a bicycle: a benchmark and review. Proc. R. Soc. A 463 (2007). Local copy: mubo9707.pdf. Moore, J.K. Human Control of a Bicycle. PhD thesis, UC Davis, 2012. PyDy bicycle validation example: https://github.com/pydy/pydy/tree/master/examples/bicycle_validation
